title: Conservation of Energy
lead: Energy is conserved: whatever forms it passes through, the total at the end of a process equals the total at the start. The law adds one term to the mechanical energy and the nonconservative work for every other kind of energy a system holds. You meet the forms energy takes beyond the mechanical ones, follow energy through the conversions that go on all the time, and define the efficiency of a conversion as the share of the input that comes out as useful work.
objectives: Explain the law of the conservation of energy.
Describe some of the many forms of energy.
Define efficiency of an energy conversion process as the fraction left as useful energy or work, rather than being transformed, for example, into thermal energy.
summary_html:
• The law of conservation of energy states that the total energy is constant in any process. Energy may change in form or be transferred from one system to another, but the total remains the same.
  • When all forms of energy are considered, conservation of energy is written in equation form as $\kKEi + \kPEi + \kWnc + \kOEi = \kKEf + \kPEf + \kOEf$, where $\kOE$ is all other forms of energy besides mechanical energy.
  • Commonly encountered forms of energy include electric energy, chemical energy, radiant energy, nuclear energy, and thermal energy.
  • Energy is often utilized to do work, but it is not possible to convert all the energy of a system to work.
  • The efficiency $\text{Eff}$ of a machine or human is defined to be $\text{Eff} = \frac{\kWout}{\kEin}$, where $\kWout$ is useful work output and $\kEin$ is the energy consumed.
notes: The third problem, on how many nine-megaton fusion bombs a year’s energy needs would take, has no answer in the book’s key and is left out, and the link to the PhET Masses and Springs laboratory is left out as the book’s other interactive links are.

exercises.prompt: You do 30 J of work to load a toy dart gun. However, the dart is 10 cm long and feels a frictional force of 10 N while going through the dart gun’s barrel. What is the kinetic energy of the fired dart?

answer.hint: The work you did to load the gun is stored in the spring, and friction acts on the dart over the length of the barrel, so write the account with a term for the work done against friction.

exercises.prompt: When an object is lifted by a crane, it begins and ends its motion at rest. The same is true of an object pushed across a rough surface. Explain why this happens. What are the differences between these systems?

answer.solution: In both cases the object starts at rest and ends at rest, so the change in its kinetic energy over the whole motion is zero. By the work-energy theorem the net work on it is zero, although work certainly happens. The crane’s cable does positive work on the load while gravity does an equal negative work, and the push does positive work on the object while friction does an equal negative work. The two systems differ in where the energy goes. Gravity is conservative, so the work done against it becomes gravitational potential energy, and lowering the load gets it back. The load sits higher, and the mechanical energy of the load-Earth system has risen by exactly the crane’s work. Friction is nonconservative, so the work done against it leaves as thermal energy in the surface and the object, and no change of position returns it. The mechanical energy of that system is unchanged, and the energy the push put in is now other energy.

exercises.prompt: A child has two red wagons, with the rear one tied to the front by a stretchy rope (a spring). If the child pulls on the front wagon, the ____ increases.

options: potential energy stored in the spring
answer.hint: Ask what the child’s work goes into: the wagons are moving faster than they were, and the rope between them is stretched further than it was.

exercises.prompt: A child has two red wagons, with the rear one tied to the front by a stretchy rope (a spring). If the child pulls on the front wagon, the energy stored in the system increases. How do the relative amounts of potential and kinetic energy in this system change over time?

answer.solution: At the first tug the front wagon moves before the rear one, so the rope stretches, and most of the child’s energy goes into potential energy in the rope while the rear wagon is still nearly at rest. The stretched rope then pulls the rear wagon forward: the stretch falls and the wagon speeds up, turning the rope’s potential energy into kinetic energy of the wagons. The rope acts as a spring, so the rear wagon overshoots, the rope goes slack, and the wagon falls behind and stretches it again. The two forms trade back and forth as the pair rolls along. The total keeps rising, since the child keeps doing work on the front wagon, but its split at any moment depends on the rope’s stretch. Friction in the wheels and losses in the rope turn part of the total into thermal energy all the while, so the mechanical share falls the longer the pull lasts.

exercises.prompt:
Which of the following are closed systems?
  1. Earth
  2. a car
  3. a frictionless pendulum
  4. a mass on a spring in a vacuum
Describe a real-world example of a closed system.

answer.solution: Look for something whose boundary no energy crosses: nothing goes in and nothing leaks out. No real system is perfectly closed, so any example holds only over a time short enough that what does cross does not matter. A stoppered vacuum flask of hot coffee is a good one, because the vacuum between its walls carries away almost no thermal energy, and the energy inside stays nearly constant for an hour or two. A heavy bob swinging on a long wire inside a sealed, evacuated case is another, since it has no air to rub against and little friction at the support. The Earth is a poor choice, because the Sun pours radiant energy onto it all day and the Earth radiates energy back into space all night. Whichever example you choose, say where your system’s boundary is and what would have to cross it for the system to stop being closed.

exercises.prompt: A 5.0-kg rock falls off of a 10 m cliff. If air resistance exerts an average force of 10 N, what is the kinetic energy when the rock hits the ground?

answer.hint: The potential energy the rock loses is $mgh$, and air resistance takes a force multiplied by the same distance away from it; one of the four options is not even an energy.

exercises.prompt: Hydroelectricity is generated by storing water behind a dam, and then letting some of it run through generators in the dam to turn them. If the system is the water, what is the environment that is doing work on it? If a dam has water 100 m deep behind it, how much energy was generated if 10,000 kg of water exited the dam at 2.0 m/s?

answer.solution: The environment does work on the water through the gravitational force of the Earth. As the water falls, the gravitational potential energy of the water-Earth system converts to other forms, which is the same as saying that gravity does work on the water. For the second part, take the water 100 m up behind the dam as the initial state and the water leaving the outlet at 2.0 m/s as the final state. Its potential energy at the start, measured from the outlet, is $\kPEg = m\kg\kh = (10{,}000\ \text{kg})(9.80\ \text{m/s}^2)(100\ \text{m})$, and it starts at rest, so that is all its energy. The energy it still carries as it leaves is $\kKE = \tfrac{1}{2}m\kv^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}(10{,}000\ \text{kg})(2.0\ \text{m/s})^2$. The generators have taken whatever the water no longer has, so the energy generated is the first number less the second. Friction in the pipes would take some more, but the question gives no way to work it out and asks you to neglect it.

figure.caption: A car experiencing non-negligible friction coasts down a hill, over a small crest, then downhill again, and comes to a stop at a gas station.

exercises.prompt: Consider the following scenario. A car for which friction is not negligible accelerates from rest down a hill, running out of gasoline after a short distance. The driver lets the car coast farther down the hill, then up and over a small crest. He then coasts down that hill into a gas station, where he brakes to a stop and fills the tank with gasoline. Identify the forms of energy the car has, and how they are changed and transferred in this series of events.

answer.solution: Follow the car through the run and name what it has at every stage. At the top it is at rest, so it has gravitational potential energy and no kinetic energy, and the gasoline in its tank carries chemical energy. Down the first hill the engine turns part of that chemical energy into kinetic energy, and the potential energy of the car-Earth system becomes kinetic energy too. Friction in the drivetrain and tires and the drag of the air turn part of both into thermal energy, warming the car and the air. Once the gasoline runs out, the only exchange is between gravitational potential energy and kinetic energy, less what friction keeps taking. Coasting up over the crest, the car trades kinetic energy for potential energy and slows. Down the second hill it takes it back and speeds up. Braking at the gas station turns all the remaining kinetic energy into thermal energy in the brakes. Filling the tank moves chemical energy into the car from outside, a transfer between systems rather than a change of form. At no stage does energy disappear: what one form gives up, another takes.

exercises.prompt: Describe the energy transfers and transformations for a javelin, starting from the point at which an athlete picks up the javelin and ending when the javelin is stuck into the ground after being thrown.

answer.solution: The chemical energy in the athlete’s muscles is the source of all of it. Picking up the javelin and carrying it to the mark, the athlete turns a little of that energy into the gravitational potential energy of the raised javelin and the kinetic energy of the run-up. Most becomes thermal energy in the body, which is only about a fifth efficient. In the throw the athlete does work on the javelin over the length of the arm and the turn of the body, so more chemical energy becomes the javelin’s kinetic energy. In flight the javelin trades kinetic energy for potential energy as it rises and takes it back as it falls, while air resistance turns a small part into thermal energy in the javelin and the air. When the point strikes, the kinetic energy goes into pushing the soil apart, into thermal energy in the soil and the shaft, and into sound. The javelin ends at rest, lower than it started, and every joule it began with is somewhere else.

exercises.prompt: Do devices with efficiencies of less than one violate the law of conservation of energy? Explain.

answer.solution: No. An efficiency of less than one says that only part of the energy put in comes out as useful work, not that the rest of it has gone away. The conservation law is about the total, and the total is the same as it was: what does not come out as useful work leaves as thermal energy in the device and the air around it, and as sound and light. A gasoline engine whose efficiency is 30 percent turns three tenths of the chemical energy in its fuel into the work of driving the car, and the other seven tenths leaves through the radiator and the exhaust pipe as thermal energy. The efficiency counts only the useful share; the conservation law counts every joule.

exercises.prompt: List four different forms or types of energy. Give one example of a conversion from each of these forms to another form.

answer.solution: Electrical, chemical, radiant, nuclear and thermal energy are five forms beyond the mechanical ones, and any four will do. An electric motor turns electrical energy into the mechanical energy of a turning shaft. An engine turns the chemical energy in gasoline into thermal energy and then mechanical energy, and a person climbing stairs turns the chemical energy in food into kinetic and potential energy. A solar cell turns radiant energy from the Sun into electrical energy, and a leaf turns it into chemical energy by photosynthesis. A reactor core turns nuclear energy into thermal energy, and the generator its steam drives turns that into electrical energy. A turbine turns the thermal energy of a boiler’s steam into mechanical energy. In each case name the starting form and the final form, and say what does the converting.

exercises.prompt: List the energy conversions that occur when riding a bicycle.

answer.solution: The rider’s food is the source, so the chain begins with chemical energy in the muscles. The legs turn it into mechanical work on the pedals, and about four fifths of it becomes thermal energy in the rider at the same time, since cycling is about 20 percent efficient. The work on the pedals becomes the kinetic energy of rider and bicycle as they speed up, and gravitational potential energy whenever the road climbs. Coming down a hill, that potential energy turns back into kinetic energy. Friction in the chain and bearings and the drag of the air turn part of the kinetic energy into thermal energy the whole time, so the rider must pedal to hold a steady speed on level ground. Braking turns the rest of the kinetic energy into thermal energy in the brake blocks and rims. A dynamo, if fitted, turns a little of the mechanical energy into electrical energy and then into the lamp’s radiant energy.

exercises.prompt: Using values from Table 7.1, how many DNA molecules could be broken by the energy carried by a single electron in the beam of an old-fashioned TV tube? (These electrons were not dangerous in themselves, but they did create dangerous x rays. Later model tube TVs had shielding that absorbed x rays before they escaped and exposed viewers.)

answer.hint: Read the energy of a single electron in the beam and the energy needed to break one DNA strand off Table 7.1, and divide the first by the second.

exercises.prompt: Using energy considerations and assuming negligible air resistance, show that a rock thrown from a bridge 20.0 m above water with an initial speed of 15.0 m/s strikes the water with a speed of 24.8 m/s independent of the direction thrown.

(a) Use of hydrogen fusion to supply energy is a dream that may be realized in the next century. Fusion would be a relatively clean and almost limitless supply of energy, as can be seen from Table 7.1. To illustrate this, calculate how many years the present energy needs of the world could be supplied by one millionth of the oceans’ hydrogen fusion energy. (b) How does this time compare with historically significant events, such as the duration of stable economic systems?

answer.hint: Table 7.1 gives the fusion energy of all the hydrogen in the oceans and the annual world energy use; take a millionth of the first and divide by the second.
answer.solution: (a) $25 \times 10^{6}\ \text{years}$ (b) This is much, much longer than human time scales.
